{"docket_number": "84-468", "additional_docket_numbers": null, "term": "1984", "first_party": "City of Cleburne, Texas", "first_party_label": "Petitioner", "second_party": "Cleburne Living Center, Inc.", "second_party_label": "Respondent", "manner_of_jurisdiction": "Writ of certiorari", "lower_court": "United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit", "argued": ["1985-03-18T06:00:00Z"], "question": "

Did the denial of the permit violate the Equal Protection rights of Cleburne Living Center, Inc. and its potential residents?

", "facts_of_the_case": "

In 1980, Cleburne Living Center, Inc. submitted a permit application to operate a home for the mentally retarded. The city council of Cleburne voted to deny the special use permit, acting pursuant to a municipal zoning ordinance.

", "conclusion": "

In a unanimous judgment, the Court held that the denial of the special use permit to Cleburne Living Centers, Inc. was premised on an irrational prejudice against the mentally retarded, and hence unconstitutional under the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. While the Court declined to grant the mentally retarded the status of a "quasi-suspect class," it nevertheless found that the "rational relation" test for legislative action provided sufficient protection against invidious discrimination.

analysis.body: {"transcript": {"text": "City of Cleburne against Cleburne Living Center. Mr. Luna, you may proceed whenever you're ready. Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the court, this case presents the questions of whether mentally retarded persons constitute a quasi-suspect class for purposes of equal protection analysis and whether legislation, such as the City of Cleburne's ordinance, in this case, must be tested by an intermediate or heightened level of scrutiny. First, I'd like to discuss the concept of quasi-suspect status in regard to the mentally retarded. The primary criteria for determination of suspectness was articulated by this court in Frontero v. Richardson. The court stated that what differentiates sex from such non-suspect statuses as intelligence and physical disability and aligns it with recognized suspect criteria is that the sex characteristic frequently bears no relation to the ability to perform or to contribute to society. In declining to join in adding sex as a suspect class, the concurrent opinion stated that it seems to me that this reaching out to preempt by judicial action a major political decision, which is currently in the process of resolution, does not reflect appropriate respect for duly prescribed legislative processes. Now, there has been a considerable amount of legislation in the area of the mentally retarded, and it continues to pin before the legislatures of most states as well as the Congress of the United States. In Massachusetts' Board of Retirement v. Mergier, in a procuriam opinion, this court held that age was not a suspect class and, in doing so, observed that it had not been subjected to the unique disabilities on the basis of stereotype characteristics not truly indicative of their disabilities. Now, the Third Circuit heeded Frontero and Mergier in deciding that mentally ill persons were not a suspect class in Doe v. Colada. Although mental retardation differs from the mentally ill, the rationale of the relationship between the actual disability and the stereotype characterizations is applicable to at least some of the mentally retarded. Doe v. Colada formed the basis for the district court's opinion in this case, and although dealing with the mentally ill rather than the mentally retarded, the reasoning in that case is directly related and applicable to the case at Barr. The Third Circuit in the Doe case stated that although the mentally ill have been victims of stereotypes, the disabilities imposed on them often reflected that many of the mentally ill do have reduced ability for personal relations, for economic activity, and for political choice. Now, that, of course, is different from some of the other suspect classes that the court has found to be suspect that's not related to their ability to perform and contribute to society. A classification based on mental retardation fails the threshold analysis, since by the very definition, it is sub-average general intellectual functioning existing concurrently with deficits in adaptive behavior. It's a problem of reduced ability to learn, difficulty with abstract thinking, judgment, problem-solving, and retention, and includes problems of social adjustment and economic productivity. In other words, the mentally retarded do have a diminished ability to function in society and a diminished productivity. The cases have specifically addressed the suspect or quasi-suspect status for the mentally retarded or the handicap, which includes, of course, the mentally retarded, and they've been clear and unequivocal, we think, in their holdings. This court in Youngberg v. Romeo in dealing with institutionalized, mentally retarded persons, explicitly refused to apply a compelling or a substantial test and applied a professional judgment test to the mentally retarded in that case. The lower court had applied the heightened scrutiny test, and this court set aside that decision went on the professional basis test, the professional advice test. Mr. Luna, would you tell us again what objectives the city has in this particular ordinance as applied to the home for the retarded? Under the police powers of the state that are delegated to the city, the city has a responsibility of protecting people and seeing to it that they have a safe environment. Therefore, in this case, the city refused a special use permit for mainly the following reasons. Number one, there were too many people in this particular house. Well, you still take the position that the only purpose is to protect the health and safety of the residents of the group home. Health and safety of the residents is the only reason. No other purpose. No other purpose. Our testimony showed that we had some people in the neighborhood that complained but the health, who objected to it because they were afraid of it. Okay, and so before us today, that's the only purpose on which you rely. Right. And the state attorney general tells us that the state of Texas has preempted that determination and that under state law, the state will decide on what is a safe environment for the retarded in a group home. Attorney General... How do we deal with that? The attorney general, we think, did not take a look at the regulations. As a matter of fact, the regulations that the state of Texas puts out will not permit this home to be placed in a city unless that city does have a requirement of a special use permit or other zoning law. So contrary to what the attorney general is saying in this amicus curia brief, the facts are, and it is in evidence here, the facts are that the state requires them to place these homes only in a city that has a special use permit or other... Does the state go ahead and spell out what requirements the city should have in granting the permit? It does not. Now, it does set out some minimum standards standards that the home must have before the state will approve it, but it has none as far as the city is concerned. And of course, in our state, the reason we are going to neighborhood living is because the state standards have been completely to minimum and have failed. And we are moving people out or attempting to move them out of the state homes and the state institutions and put them in the communities, but the city of Cleburne says that normal living in Cleburne means safety, living in a way where 13 of them with two and a half baths attempting to get to a work center, incidentally, a city of 20,000 people, there are not many that has a work center for the mentally retarded like Cleburne does. We have 30 mentally retarded across the street from this very facility. They wanted to locate this facility in this home across the street from a junior high where the parents are bringing the kids to school and taking them away. The city, the evidence showed, recommended to them another facility. They declined to put it in the other facility and when asked isn't the only reason you didn't put it in the other facility was because it would cut down your profits and the answer in the record was no, then why didn't you? The answer was because the project couldn't stand the burden of the additional cost. Now, we submit that it is necessary for them to provide a safe environment and that that is the responsibility of the city to require that we do have a safe environment for, of all people, mentally retarded people, and this group of mentally retarded people are people who did not have the skills of independent living. In the Youngberg case, this court declined to institute the compelling or substantial reason and the court said that it would be unduly burdensome on the state to make that kind of requirement. This court's dismissal of the appeal in Macon Association versus Macon-Bibb County upheld the determination that the mentally retarded were not a suspect class. And even the Fifth Circuit in Brown versus Sibley, although it changed its mind in this case, held that applying the rational basis review to a state agency's policy against the visually impaired working in supervisory position, held that no court has ever declared that handicapped persons constitute a suspect class for purposes of equal protection analysis, and we decline to do so today. The case of the California Association of the Physically Handicapped case that we cite in our brief, CERT, was denied by this court in 1984, again applied the rational basis review to the FCC's refusal to include the handicap in its EEO program, and in doing so, the Ninth Circuit said that no appellate court, however, has held that the handicapped or a suspect class we decline to be the first. Other indicia of suspectness are summarized in San Antonio versus Rodriguez's case as a class saddled with such disabilities or subjected to such a history of purposeful unequal treatment or relegated to such a position of political power and to command extraordinary protection from the majoritarian political process. In Texas, we had the question raised last time with regard to permitting people to vote. The Texas statute is the Election Code, Article 5.01, permits anybody to vote who is registered under the age of 18 years of age and who are not mentally incompetent as determined by a final judgment of a court. And there's some other things about a felony conviction, but Texas permits the mentally retarded to vote if they register, if they're 18 years old, unless they have been declared incompetent by some court. Now, we think that the court in Rodriguez in its holding was actually used some language that applies directly to our case when the court prescribed the recognition of a class that was large, diverse, and amorphous, the opposite of discrete, insular minority. That was the type that was envisioned by the court in the U.S. v. Carolyn Products. A class dealing with illegitimacy is, of course, different because the immutable trait is not one, in that case, that has anything to do with their ability to produce or to contribute to society, and this court in Parham v. Hughes in 1979 is so recognized. While mental retardation is immutable, it's relevant to classification like other immutable characteristics, such as blindness. In Upshur v. Love, a Northern District California case, 1979, 474, Feb, Sup, 332, the court held that the visually handicapped were not entitled to suspect status because classifications based on blindness often can be justified by the different abilities of the blind and the sighted. And that, of course, is the situation with the mentally retarded people because if heightened scrutiny should be applied to legislation involving the mentally retarded, what standard should we apply? The mentally retarded with an IQ below 70 and a deficit in adaptive behavior are a diverse group within themselves, and they consist of several subgroups. The mildly mentally retarded constitute approximately 89% of all of the mentally retarded persons. Add to that the moderately retarded and the severely retarded, both of the manifestations of retardation and the level of care required by each of the subgroup varies to a great extreme. Some of them require no care. Some require institutionalization. Now, more than half of the mildly mentally retarded, our record show, melt into society, and after they leave school, you never know that they are mentally retarded. So as to that group, the only way one could know that that person is mentally retarded is to have an opportunity to know what their IQ is, and in addition to that, have the advice of an expert who could tell us that the person had a deficit in adaptive behavior. Unless one had those things, a person does not even know who those mentally retarded persons are. Yet, they're tossed in with one group that the Fifth Circuit has held should have heightened scrutiny to all legislation, and if it's only reasonable and rational, it is not sufficient. Under the Fifth Circuit requirement, the mentally retarded are placed in a catch-22 situation. Since their needs are so different, the government can only address those needs by establishing classifications based on mental retardation and provide differing benefits for different groups of mentally retarded people. Yet, the classification would fail if it's only reasonable and rational. Where they're trying to do something for the group, the legislation would fail if it's only reasonable and rational. Even the case that we're here on today, those mentally retarded people who were prospective people who would live in that home could not be there except for the fact that they have been classified as mentally retarded and it's a federally funded Medicaid contract with the state of Texas which permits them to be there because they are being treated differently. Hack and scrutiny is not the answer to the problems of the mentally retarded. The legislative approach, as was mentioned in Frontero, if left unhampered, will provide for the needs of the mentally retarded. It's doing so now at all levels of government. That position has been articulated by the Solicitor General in the government's brief in this case. We believe that the action of the city of Cleaver has shown that that legislation is helping and is to the benefit of the mentally retarded. because the national policy being to restore them to normal neighborhood living, that type of living, with 13 people to two bathrooms, with four people and four unrelated adults in one bedroom, is not normal in very many neighborhoods in anybody's community. It is bound to create the same type of transplanted, overcrowded condition into the cities that we have in the states right now, and we will have gained nothing except scattered the problem out if we don't permit the cities to require those people to have at least humane conditions in those homes. A contractor is, if a contractor can keep putting more people in one home at less cost, it's to that contractor's advantage. The city of Cleburne, and of course we are the first ones to recognize people's rights and needs to make a profit, but not at the expense of inhumane treatment to a bunch of people who cannot take care of themselves. Mr. Luna, has the city given a permit or license to any other group home for the retarded in the city of Cleburne? The city has not given a permit for a mentally retarded home because this is the only one that has ever been applied for. They tried to get this group to apply for a permit at a different location this group refused. This is the only permit that's ever been applied for. So as far as a place to live in the city of Cleburne out in the community for the retarded, there just isn't one, I take it. Oh, yes. They're not in a group home simply because nobody has made an application except this one. They'd have to be institutionalized then in your community. We have 30 people, we have 30 mentally retarded students in the junior high school across the street from this place. We have a lot of mentally retarded. Now, they can live, if they're mentally retarded people who can live in a boarding house, for example, they can live any place they want to. The only restriction here is that small group of mentally retarded people who don't have the skills of independent living. The others can live any place they want to in the city of Cleburne, and they're no problem with it. It's been, I think, that the respondents have attempted to say that this ordinance keeps mentally retarded people out of Cleburne. It does not. And this record is replete with evidence where the respondents were asked to apply on property different from this, property that would comply with the health and sanitation requirements of the city of Cleburne. Heightened scrutiny is, we think, especially inappropriate for zoning ordinance. A zoning ordinance is one that, of course, uses classifications as the very basis of the zoning ordinance. This court has established a long history, commenced with Village of Euclis versus Amber Realty in 1926, through its recent recent cases like Village of Beltaire versus Boras, and a recent case by Mr. Justice Stevens and the members of the City Council of Los Angeles versus the taxpayers of Vincent in applying the rational basis test to zoning classification unless the ordinance was racially exclusive. Otherwise, if it's fairly debatable or any set of facts reasonably may be conceived to justify, it must be allowed to stand. Now, in this case, I think it's important, and I've mentioned it before, to realize the kind of people we had on this city council. We had people, and one thing, we are amazed at some of the groups that are on the other side of this case. We had a person who believed, he's deceased now, who believed he knew something about discrimination. He was a black man. He also was a person who was on the board of directors of the mentally retarded workshop that's in the city of Cleburne and has had a history of working with them and helping them for many years. And he felt that these people were not being treated properly and they deserve more. The second of the three people who voted for this particular denial of this particular permit was a man who had a mentally retarded granddaughter. Her life was short, but her memory is like that of all of us who lose relatives at a young age. What has that got to do with this case? Sir? What does that have to do with this case? I think what it has to do is in their answer where they say that this was not a rational basis for this ordinance. And this shows it is. Sir? To find out what the people are and whether they're black or white or whether they have relatives or not proves that point. I think to know what the people intended is the whole crux of this. Whether the council here was attempting to discriminate or whether the council was attempting to do something that was good and protective for the people. I believe that's an important part. I may be wrong. But I think what the city was trying to accomplish is a part of the rational basis and that is why it is a debatable question. And this court has held in all of these cases that if it is a debatable reason then the ordinance will stand insofar as the rational basis is concerned. Mr. Luna, in the Texas brief, I had a question if I may. Your argument based on the zoning powers that you made a moment or two ago, the Texas brief suggests that the zoning power in Texas at least is properly used to protect adjoining property owners and the public at large rather than the people who aren't being able to use the property for the purpose they want to use it for. Are there cases that sustain the exercise of zoning power to protect the property owner who is denied the right to use the property the way he wants to? Oh, yes, sir. Many of them. Of course, that's why the zoning laws require sprinklers in buildings. That's not going to hurt the folks next door, but it's going to hurt the users. There are many, many situations. Well, I know there are many regulations that protect the person, but the zoning laws, you say, there are too. Oh, yes, sir. They are in the zoning law themselves. May I ask this question, Mr. Luna? The ordinance, as I understand it, includes mentally retarded in the category with alcoholics and drug addicts. Is that correct? It does mention them in the same paragraph with alcoholics and drug addicts. And the only other category listed are feeble-minded, and they are construed, I take it, to include the parties involved in this case. Mentally retarded people. Yes, sir. Are they insane and drug addicts required to obtain a special use permit to occupy a home? No, sir. Not homes. Well, does that mean that only the mentally retarded are required to obtain a special permit? No. For a special use permit for a home, for the drug addicts, and for special use permits, they would have to. So alcoholics and drug addicts are required to obtain a special permit? Yes, sir. Has a special permit been issued on any application filed by either of those groups? I can't answer that. Our record does not reflect. Do you know of any other special permit other than the one that's before us today? The one that's before us today, insofar as the mentally retarded is concerned, is the only one that has been applied for. Yes. There's not another one on record. How long has the ordinance been in effect? I don't recall. I think the brief state... The ordinance has been in effect since about, I believe, in the 60s. But we have only had the movement in Texas over the last few years to, as in most other states, to attempt to move the mentally retarded out of the state institution. Will you summarize again for me the state interest that requires a special permit for the mentally retarded? Putting them in the same category with drug addicts and insane people. Well, and I would also put them in the same one, on down in that same paragraph, you have to run a nursery. You also, to run a nursery for, to keep rid of children, you also have to get a special use permit. So it doesn't put them just with the drug addicts and alcoholics. Are the standards directed at the capacity of people to take care of themselves? And the ones that have to get the special use permit, most of them are not able to take care of themselves. There are a few instances where they are, drive-in theaters included in it, and golf clubs and a few things like that. But nursery schools and cemeteries, drug addicts, alcoholics, and a number of them, it's a matter, we think, of classification and not at all discrimination. Did you identify the state interest in response to my question? No, sir. I'd be glad to know. Right. The state interest is that we're dealing with only the limited group of mentally retarded people who do not have the skills of independent living. That's the only ones that are involved here. What state purpose is served by this restriction on this category of people? What is that restriction? What state interest is served by the restriction on the feeble-minded? Well, under the Medicaid contract, this is federally funded contract, the respondent has a contract with the state to keep only those people. Now, our state interest is that those people who can't take care of themselves should not be on a street right across the street from a junior high school. And they ought to be placed in a facility that will have room, more sleeping room, than four in a bedroom. And they are attempting to teach them rehabilitation training. They leave and are supposed to be at the training station at 8 o'clock in the morning. 13 of them. It would be awfully difficult for them to take 13 of them to take a bath. In this particular facility, I was speaking generally during the ordinance on its face. I think you've answered the question sufficiently. Thank you very much. Thank you. Thank you. Mr. Hicks. Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the court, I think that after five years now, the city has finally narrowed what its positive objectives are in this case to a simple one. It is, apparently, although I'm not quite sure. Mr. Hicks, suppose you had a situation where in this same house you had 26 people. It was proposed to use it for 26 people of the same category. Would you be here? I don't think we would be here, Your Honor, because the state Medicaid rules would not allow 26 people under their space requirements. I'm not supposed to. It's 20 people. Again, I don't think the state Medicaid rules would allow it. I haven't calculated what the square footage requirements and other requirements under the state Medicaid rules are that would set an upper limit. I think it's around 15, if I remember correctly. Well, then, doesn't this come down to a question of judgment of the people on the ground, knowing the environment and the conditions, and their judgment as to how many people can safely and appropriately be in on a establishment of this kind, given all the other conditions? No, Your Honor, I don't think it does. The reason I don't think it does is because that was not the judgment that was made. There is no indication, I don't think the slightest indication, in the city zoning ordinance that this discrimination in Section 8, Subdivision 6, singling out mentally retarded people that are going to live in group homes for different treatment, was intended to protect them. The closest thing to an indication of an objective would be in the special use permit provision, and there the only objective mentioned is impacts on neighboring property values, and that is something the city has agreed. It is not trying to further through the classification here. I think that the standards the city has established, if you consider them carefully, looking at the record here, and I think it's important to keep in mind that this decision was reached by a city council, the votes of three city council members who admitted at trial that they don't know what mental retardation is and what it entails, that the standards that they set... Should they be experts in order to vote? I don't think they have to be experts, Your Honor. They have to know something about it? I think they have to know something about it, or at least be willing to listen to those that do. Do you think we have to qualify in order to vote here? To qualify as experts, Your Honor? No, I don't. We don't qualify as much as they had to be. You think they had to be qualified? Well, Your Honor, I think the court is willing to learn something about mental retardation from the people that discuss it in briefs and mechus briefs or in general treatises. The city council members here, as they admitted at trial, had no interest in that, and they ignored the advice of the phalanx of people opposed to what they were doing. The people opposed to what the city council did, that is, denied a special use permit, were composed of parents, of retarded people that would live there, people who had spent their lives working in this area, and none of them agreed with what the city council did. There was not one person who knew anything about mental retardation who said the city council acted properly in denying the special use permit. Well, Mr. Hicks, if we were to apply a rational basis standard, the court doesn't normally look at how much the legislative body knew about a subject. It seems to me that we look at whether there is any possible legitimate state objective and whether the provision is rationally related to that. Now, isn't that true? If that were the test, the standard of review. Well, I think the court does not merely accept any positive state objective if the ordinance or the matter under consideration, the piece of legislation under consideration, indicates that that could not possibly have been an objective. And I think this one does. First of all, it indicates that this one could not possibly have been. The city is asserting today that its purpose was to protect the health and well-being and safety of the inhabitants of the group home. I mean, that's what I understood Mr. Luna to be saying. I understand that's what they're saying. They're saying it now. That is not what they've said through most of this case. And it's very important that the whole structure of this zoning ordinance gives no indication that that was the objective. And it's impossible for somebody to try to determine what kind of group home would be acceptable if you don't know until five years later that that is the objective. Well, I guess what troubles me is that in most of our rational basis test cases, the court is willing to indulge whatever might be conceived of as a legitimate purpose in order to test it. Right? Well, I think the court is split on that. If my reading of the cases is correct, there are some instances in which the court isn't looking to whatever somebody in their wildest imagination could come up with as an objective. They also look, I think as Justice Powell mentioned in his dissent in Schwecker v. Wilson, to see whether the statute at issue actually had this as a possible objective. Well, you're really asking if we don't adopt heightened scrutiny to at least apply a rational basis test with teeth in it. Yes, and I think the majority of the court has said that the rational basis test has teeth. The court, in several cases over the last 15 years, has applied the rational basis test and invalidated certain laws. And I think it's important for the court to notice what standards the city has in effect established here to protect mentally retarded people that are going to live in group homes. The standards are no more specific than this, and I think this is a fair reading of the record. When it comes to proximity to schools, the standard is the school's too near. When it comes to how busy are the streets, the standard is, oh, the streets are too busy. When it comes to the size of the group home, it comes to the home's too small. That is as close to a specific objective as the city or standard is the city set in all this. And I think that boils down to one standard, and that is, this is reading the city's position, I think, in the best light possible. That standard is nothing's good enough for a group home. Mr. Hicks, if the ordinance is facially valid... Facially invalid? If it is facially valid, do you think you can defend it on an as-applied basis in view of the overcrowding of 13 people mentally retarded with two and a half bathrooms and only four bedrooms? Would you defend it as applied, assuming the facial validity of the statute? Yes, Your Honor, I would. I think it would be quite an adequate group home. The best sometimes can be enemy of the good, I think. There can be better group homes. There can be smaller group homes with more space. But I think it is perfectly defensible. It meets state rules set up for these programs under a federal program. And the court quite often looks to federal standards that have been established to determine what the prevailing mores of society are in terms of what's acceptable. Let's assume the state of Texas... You applied for a license with the state people? Yes. And suppose the state of Texas said, Sorry, but 13 beds are too many. You can only have six. Yes. Would you apply your heightened scrutiny to that kind of a rule and attack it on a constitutional basis? Well, I don't think there would be intentional discrimination in that situation against mentally retarded people. They would just be making an individual judgment in an individual case that are based on standards that are... But you would say that there would be... You would say that the state must have a rational reason for making that rule? I think that there must be a rational basis, yes. One of the amicus briefs says that... It says that... That... The case is moot because after the date that you filed your petition, the Texas Human Resources Department modified its regulations to limit these residents to six beds. Is that true? Is it true that it's moot? It's not moot. Well, I didn't ask you. Did they... Have they changed their rule to six beds? They have changed... The state Medicaid rules, the last I have read them, was that there could be up to six beds in a facility. But not 13. No, that's not correct. Except when this money is going to state institutions, like state schools for mentally retarded people, in which case they have no limit on the number of beds. Some of those places have 1,000 beds, for instance. Well... So, no. It is not true that it... I just ask you, if you had filed your petition today, under the present rules, could you get the license? If the Clever and Living Center people that were going to open the group home, I don't think so. Well, then, what's this case all about? Well, the case... I mean, you can't... I would... And there's no grandfather clause in these regulations. Well, in the record, there is evidence that indicates that this is grandfather. This particular group home has been grandfathered. The administrator of the program, the Department of Human Resources program, which promulgates the rules, has said that this group home is not subject to those rules because it had filed its application before May 1, 19... Was this fact before the Court of Appeals? Yes. That these rules have been changed? Yes. This whole matter has been in the case from the beginning. And the group home... This group home could open today if the Court were to rule that the city... Only because you filed it before the rule was changed. Yes. But I still think, Your Honor, that that doesn't indicate that the city hasn't discriminated against mentally retarded people, which is what this case is about. This case, I don't think, is about whether state Medicaid rules are valid or applicable here.
